questions.question: What is the purpose of a checksum in the context of Amazon S3?

options.text: To encrypt files during upload
To generate a unique fingerprint that detects any byte-level data corruption
To compress files before storage
To control who can access objects

explanation.correct: A checksum processes every byte of a file sequentially and produces a fixed-length fingerprint. Even a single changed byte produces a completely different output, making corruption impossible to hide.
explanation.why: A is encryption (SSE), C is compression (not an S3 feature), D is IAM and bucket policies.

questions.question: Which four additional checksum algorithms does Amazon S3 support?

options.text: MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, CRC32
SHA-1, SHA-256, CRC32, CRC32-C
SHA-256, CRC32, CRC32-C, Adler-32
MD5, SHA-256, CRC32-C, Blake2

explanation.correct: S3 supports SHA-1, SHA-256, CRC32, and CRC32-C as additional algorithms. MD5 is used internally via ETags as the default — it is not one of the four additional options you choose.
explanation.why: MD5 is S3's default ETag mechanism. The four additional options are what you explicitly choose during upload for enhanced integrity verification.

questions.question: What AWS CLI flag enables checksum verification during an S3 upload?

options.text: --enable-checksum SHA256
--verify-integrity
--checksum-algorithm SHA256
--with-checksum SHA-256

explanation.correct: The correct flag is --checksum-algorithm SHA256 used with aws s3api put-object. The CLI calculates the hash locally, sends it in request headers, and S3 re-validates on receipt.
explanation.why: The other options are not valid AWS CLI flags. Always use the s3api subcommand (not s3) when you need checksum control.

questions.question: Which command retrieves S3 object metadata including its stored checksum WITHOUT downloading the file?

options.text: aws s3 cp s3://bucket/key --metadata-only
aws s3api get-object-metadata
aws s3api head-object --bucket B --key K
aws s3 ls s3://bucket/key --checksums

explanation.correct: head-object retrieves all object metadata — content type, size, ETag, ChecksumSHA256, etc. — without downloading the object data. Critical for at-scale integrity validation where downloading would be expensive.
explanation.why: There is no --metadata-only flag, get-object-metadata does not exist, and ls does not return checksum data.

questions.question: What happens when a precalculated checksum provided during S3 upload does not match what S3 calculates?

options.text: S3 stores both checksums for audit review
S3 accepts the upload but logs a warning to CloudTrail
S3 rejects the upload with an InvalidChecksum or BadDigest error
S3 uses your provided value and overwrites its own calculation

explanation.correct: A precalculated checksum mismatch causes S3 to immediately reject the upload. The corrupted data never reaches storage — this is the primary protection mechanism against transit corruption.
explanation.why: S3 never accepts data it cannot verify. There is no 'store both' or 'log a warning' behavior — the upload simply fails.

questions.question: In the command 'shasum -a 256 file.jpg | cut -f1 -d\ | xxd -r -p | base64', what does the xxd -r -p | base64 portion do?

options.text: Decodes the file from base64 and re-encodes it
Converts the hex checksum output to binary, then encodes it as base64 to match S3 format
Verifies the file has not been corrupted
Sends the checksum to S3 for comparison

explanation.correct: shasum outputs the hash as hex text. xxd -r -p converts that hex text to raw binary bytes. base64 then encodes those bytes — matching the format S3 uses to store and display checksums.
explanation.why: Without this conversion, the values look different even when the file is intact. S3 uses base64; shasum uses hex by default.

questions.question: What is the console size limit for providing a precalculated SHA-256 checksum value during an S3 upload?

options.text: 5 MB
16 MB
100 MB
No size limit

explanation.correct: The S3 console limits precalculated checksum input to files under 16 MB. For larger files, use AWS CLI with --checksum-sha256 or AWS SDK, which have no such restriction.
explanation.why: This is a console limitation only, not a service limitation. Production systems always use CLI or SDK for large file uploads.

questions.question: Which checksum algorithm offers the best performance for large-scale S3 data migrations due to hardware acceleration?

options.text: SHA-256
SHA-1
CRC32
CRC32-C

explanation.correct: CRC32-C (Castagnoli) uses a polynomial optimized for hardware-level acceleration in modern CPUs and SSDs, making it the fastest S3 checksum option — recommended for high-throughput migrations.
explanation.why: CRC32-C is not cryptographic (unlike SHA-256) but offers the best raw performance. SHA-256 is the choice when cryptographic strength is required for compliance.

questions.question: In a versioning-enabled S3 bucket, what happens when you delete an object using aws s3 rm?

options.text: The object and all its versions are permanently deleted
Only the current version is deleted
A delete marker is created; all versions including the latest are preserved and recoverable
The object is automatically moved to S3 Glacier

explanation.correct: A delete in a versioned bucket places a delete marker as the latest version, making the object appear gone. All actual data versions remain intact and can be restored by removing the delete marker or retrieving a specific version ID.
explanation.why: This design means accidental deletion is always recoverable in a versioned bucket — the data is never immediately destroyed.

questions.question: What is the correct CLI command to delete a bucket AND all its contents (non-versioned bucket)?

options.text: aws s3 rb s3://bucket-name
aws s3 delete s3://bucket-name --all
aws s3 rb s3://bucket-name --force
aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket bucket-name --force

explanation.correct: aws s3 rb s3://bucket-name --force empties the bucket (deletes all objects) then deletes the bucket itself. Without --force, the command fails if the bucket is not already empty.
explanation.why: Note: --force does not handle versioned buckets well — all versions and delete markers must be removed manually using list-object-versions + delete-object for each.

questions.question: A cloud engineer's batch upload script shows 3 files with FAIL status. What is the FIRST correct action?

options.text: Immediately re-upload all 3 files to overwrite the S3 copies
Delete the affected S3 objects and re-run the script
Investigate: check if source files changed since checksum calculation, compare exact values, identify whether mismatch is local or in transit
Disable checksums and re-upload without verification

explanation.correct: Before acting, identify the cause. Was the source file modified? Was it a formatting issue (hex vs base64)? Was there a network error? Comparing the exact values tells you where the mismatch occurred. Re-uploading could overwrite a good S3 copy with a bad local file.
explanation.why: Investigate first, act second. Never overwrite without understanding the failure.

questions.question: What does ReplicationStatus 'FAILED' mean on an S3 object?

options.text: The object was successfully replicated
Replication is in progress
S3 attempted replication but could not complete it — check the replication IAM role and destination bucket permissions
The object was deleted from the source bucket

explanation.correct: FAILED means S3 tried to replicate the object but encountered an error — most commonly a missing s3:ReplicateObject permission on the replication IAM role, or a missing/misconfigured destination bucket.
explanation.why: COMPLETED = success, PENDING = queued, REPLICA = this IS the destination copy. FAILED always requires investigation.

questions.question: What is the key difference between 'aws s3 cp' and 'aws s3api put-object' for uploads?

options.text: They are identical
s3 cp is a high-level command without checksum control; s3api put-object is the low-level API command with full checksum support via --checksum-algorithm
s3api put-object is deprecated
s3 cp only works for files under 100 MB

explanation.correct: aws s3 cp is a convenience command with simplified options. aws s3api put-object maps directly to the S3 REST PutObject API, exposing all parameters including --checksum-algorithm, --checksum-sha256, metadata headers, and more.
explanation.why: For production pipelines requiring checksum verification, always use s3api put-object. s3 cp is fine for quick transfers but lacks fine-grained checksum control.

questions.question: head-object returns no ChecksumSHA256 field for an object. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: SHA-256 is not supported in this AWS region
The object was uploaded without --checksum-algorithm SHA256 or without enabling Additional checksums in the console
You need additional IAM permissions to view checksum metadata
Checksums expire after 30 days

explanation.correct: S3 only stores a checksum if explicitly requested during upload. Objects uploaded without the flag or without enabling Additional checksums in the console will not have a ChecksumSHA256 field. Re-upload with --checksum-algorithm SHA256 to add it.
explanation.why: There is no regional restriction, checksums do not expire, and no special IAM permission is needed to view them.

questions.question: Why must versioning be enabled on BOTH source AND destination buckets for Cross-Region Replication?

options.text: To reduce storage costs through deduplication
CRR has versioning as a hard prerequisite on both buckets before a replication rule can be created
Versioning is only required on the source bucket
Versioning must be enabled after replication is configured

explanation.correct: CRR requires versioning on both source and destination buckets as a hard prerequisite. If versioning is suspended on either bucket, replication stops working. Many students forget the destination bucket and encounter configuration errors.
explanation.why: This is one of the most common CRR setup mistakes. Always enable versioning on both buckets before creating the replication rule.

questions.question: What does 'cut -f1 -d\' do in the shasum checksum pipeline?

options.text: Converts hex to base64
Removes the filename from shasum's output, keeping only the hash value
Splits the file into checksum-sized chunks
Compares two checksums automatically

explanation.correct: shasum outputs two fields: the hash value and the filename separated by spaces. cut -f1 -d\ extracts only the first field (the hash), discarding the filename. Without this, comparison with S3's checksum (which has no filename) would always fail.
explanation.why: This is standard bash output parsing. -d sets delimiter (space) and -f1 selects the first field.

questions.question: A media company uploads 5TB of raw video daily. They need checksum verification but performance is critical. What is the best approach?

options.text: SHA-256 with single-part upload
CRC32-C with multipart upload
No checksum — the network is reliable enough
MD5 via ETag comparison

explanation.correct: CRC32-C is hardware-accelerated and significantly faster than SHA-256 — ideal for high-throughput media uploads. Multipart upload is required for files over 5GB and enables parallel part transfers. Together they provide both performance and integrity validation.
explanation.why: 'Network is reliable enough' is not an engineering position. MD5 via ETag is unreliable for multipart uploads because the ETag is a composite value, not a simple MD5 of the whole file.

questions.question: What IAM permission is required to upload objects to an S3 bucket using the AWS CLI?

options.text: s3:CreateObject
s3:Write
s3:PutObject
s3:UploadObject

explanation.correct: s3:PutObject is the IAM action required to upload objects to S3. Additional common permissions: s3:GetObject (download), s3:HeadObject (metadata retrieval), s3:DeleteObject (deletion), s3:ListBucket (list objects).
explanation.why: AWS uses REST verb naming — PutObject maps to HTTP PUT. There is no s3:CreateObject, s3:Write, or s3:UploadObject.

questions.question: A checksum FAIL appears in your batch script. Investigation reveals the file has Windows CRLF line endings but was processed on Linux. What likely caused the mismatch?

options.text: S3 does not support Windows file formats
CRLF to LF conversion changed the file bytes, producing a different checksum than the original Windows file
SHA-256 treats CRLF and LF identically
SHA-256 is not compatible with text files

explanation.correct: CRLF (Windows) uses 2 bytes per line ending (0x0D 0x0A), while LF (Linux) uses 1 byte (0x0A). Any conversion changes the bytes, which changes the checksum. Fix: use 'file yourfile.txt' to check line endings, and 'sed -i s/\r// yourfile.txt' to normalize before checksumming.
explanation.why: This is a real debugging scenario seen in cross-platform pipelines. The checksum is always byte-perfect — it does not know about line ending conventions.

questions.question: What does 'openssl dgst -sha256 -binary file | base64' produce, and why is it useful?

options.text: A hex checksum of the file
A base64-encoded SHA-256 checksum — the same format S3 uses — in a single cleaner pipeline without intermediate hex conversion
An encrypted version of the file
A compressed checksum of the file

explanation.correct: openssl dgst -sha256 -binary outputs the hash as raw binary bytes (skipping hex). Piping directly to base64 encodes those bytes, producing the exact base64 format S3 uses. This is a cleaner alternative to the shasum | cut | xxd | base64 pipeline.
explanation.why: 'sha256sum file | base64' would base64-encode the hex text line (including filename), producing a completely wrong result. The -binary flag is what makes this work correctly.

questions.question: A hospital must satisfy HIPAA compliance for 50,000 MRI scans per month stored in S3. Which architecture is correct?

options.text: CRC32-C checksums + S3 Standard storage
SHA-256 checksums + S3 Object Lock (WORM) + checksum records in immutable audit log (QLDB)
MD5 ETags + S3 Versioning + lifecycle to Glacier
SHA-1 checksums + Cross-Region Replication

explanation.correct: HIPAA compliance requires cryptographic proof of integrity (SHA-256), immutability to prevent deletion (Object Lock/WORM), and an auditable record independent of S3 metadata (QLDB). Storing checksums in QLDB creates a tamper-evident chain of custody.
explanation.why: CRC32-C is not cryptographic. MD5 has known weaknesses. SHA-1 is considered weak. The complete solution requires all three layers: cryptographic hash + immutability + external audit trail.

questions.question: What does '--query ChecksumSHA256 --output text' do in the head-object CLI command?

options.text: Downloads the object and calculates its SHA-256 checksum
Filters the JSON response to return only the ChecksumSHA256 value as plain text for easy variable assignment
Converts the checksum from base64 to hex
Validates the checksum against the local file

explanation.correct: --query uses JMESPath syntax to filter JSON. ChecksumSHA256 selects that field. --output text returns the raw value without JSON quotes — perfect for bash variable assignment: S3=$(aws s3api head-object --bucket B --key K --query ChecksumSHA256 --output text).
explanation.why: Without --output text, the value has JSON quotes around it, causing string comparisons in scripts to always fail.

questions.question: In a versioned bucket cleanup, why do 'aws s3 rb --force' and 'aws s3 rm --recursive' often fail to fully delete?

options.text: They are not valid for versioned buckets
They only delete the current version of each object, leaving all previous versions and delete markers in the bucket
They require admin-level IAM permissions
They work correctly for versioned buckets

explanation.correct: For versioned buckets, these commands delete only the current version — they add delete markers rather than removing all version history. Complete cleanup requires list-object-versions to get all VersionIds and DeleteMarkers, then delete-object with --version-id for each one.
explanation.why: This is a very common lab cleanup gotcha. Students run --force and think the bucket is empty, then cannot delete it because hidden versions remain.

questions.question: In multipart upload with SHA-256 checksums, Part 3 of 10 fails checksum validation. What happens?

options.text: The entire upload is cancelled and must restart from part 1
S3 rejects only part 3; the client re-uploads just that part without affecting the other 9
S3 accepts all parts and flags the object for manual review
S3 completes the upload without part 3

explanation.correct: Multipart upload validates each part independently. A failed part checksum rejects only that part. The client retries just the failed part — not the entire upload. S3 also calculates a composite checksum for the final assembled object.
explanation.why: This granular error recovery is a major advantage of multipart upload — a single corrupted 8MB part in a 10GB file requires retransmitting only 8MB, not 10GB.

questions.question: What is the correct approach for detecting post-upload corruption in S3?

options.text: Post-upload corruption is impossible — once stored, S3 data cannot change
Download the file, recalculate the checksum, and compare against the original baseline checksum recorded at upload time
Re-upload the file — if checksums match it was never corrupted
Use S3 Versioning to see if changes occurred

explanation.correct: To detect post-upload corruption, download the file, recalculate its checksum, and compare against a baseline recorded at upload time (stored in an external database or audit log). This is why maintaining independent checksum records matters — you need a baseline to compare against.
explanation.why: S3 is extremely durable but the question addresses a hypothetical scenario. Without an external baseline record, you have nothing to compare against.

questions.question: A CRR setup shows PENDING status 2 hours after upload. What should you investigate first?

options.text: PENDING after 2 hours is normal — CRR can take up to 24 hours
Check if the replication IAM role has s3:ReplicateObject permission on the destination bucket and verify versioning is active on both buckets
PENDING means the object already replicated successfully
Re-upload the files — PENDING always resolves with a re-upload

explanation.correct: Standard CRR typically completes within minutes to an hour for small files. PENDING after 2 hours usually means: missing s3:ReplicateObject on the IAM role, versioning suspended on either bucket, or the destination bucket does not exist. Enable S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) for SLA-bound workloads with 15-minute guarantees.
explanation.why: PENDING does not mean done. Check IAM role permissions first — the most common cause of replication failures.

questions.question: Which AWS service provides managed large-scale data transfer to S3 with built-in integrity checking — replacing the need for custom validation scripts?

options.text: S3 Transfer Acceleration
AWS DataSync
AWS Snowball
AWS Direct Connect

explanation.correct: AWS DataSync is a managed transfer service that automatically calculates checksums, verifies end-to-end integrity, handles retries, and provides detailed transfer reports — the managed alternative to the batch script in Extended Task 4, at enterprise scale.
explanation.why: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads (no integrity checking). Snowball is for offline petabyte migrations. Direct Connect is a network connection, not a transfer service.

questions.question: Your batch script shows 3 FAIL results. Investigation finds files were modified by auto-save between checksum calculation and upload. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Disable auto-save on the source system
Calculate checksum and upload immediately in the same script step, minimizing the modification window
Switch from SHA-256 to CRC32 — it tolerates file changes
Use --force flag to bypass checksum validation

explanation.correct: The safest approach is to calculate the checksum and upload in immediate sequence within the same loop iteration — not as two separate phases. This minimizes the window during which auto-save could modify the file. Alternatively, create a read-only snapshot of files before the validation run.
explanation.why: No checksum algorithm tolerates file changes — any change produces a completely different hash. --force does not exist for this purpose.

questions.question: A file was uploaded to S3 with --checksum-algorithm SHA256 but head-object shows ChecksumSHA256 is None. What happened?

options.text: The checksum was too long and was truncated
The upload succeeded but the --checksum-algorithm flag was silently ignored — possibly because s3 cp was used instead of s3api put-object
The bucket does not support SHA-256
The checksum was deleted by a lifecycle rule

explanation.correct: This commonly happens when students use 'aws s3 cp' thinking it supports --checksum-algorithm (it does not). Only 'aws s3api put-object' supports this flag. The upload succeeds without the flag being honored, leaving no ChecksumSHA256 in the metadata.
explanation.why: Always use s3api put-object when you need checksum control. aws s3 cp is a high-level command that does not expose all PutObject parameters.

questions.question: An enterprise backup system must prove to auditors that files have not been tampered with since upload two years ago. What architecture provides the strongest tamper-evidence?

options.text: S3 Versioning alone
SHA-256 checksums stored only in S3 object metadata
SHA-256 checksums with S3 Object Lock AND checksums independently recorded in Amazon QLDB (immutable ledger)
CRC32-C checksums with CloudTrail logging

explanation.correct: Dual chain of custody: SHA-256 provides cryptographic proof of file content; Object Lock (WORM) prevents modification or deletion of S3 objects; QLDB provides an immutable, cryptographically verified ledger of checksum records that cannot be modified even by AWS administrators. Auditors can verify QLDB independently of S3.
explanation.why: Storing checksums only in S3 metadata means a sophisticated attacker with S3 admin access could modify both the file and its metadata. QLDB's immutability is guaranteed at the service level — designed exactly for this compliance scenario.

questions.question: Which AWS service can you use to audit every S3 PutObject API call, including the checksum algorithm used?

options.text: AWS Config
Amazon CloudWatch Logs
AWS CloudTrail
AWS Trusted Advisor

explanation.correct: AWS CloudTrail records every S3 API call including PutObject, including request parameters such as the checksum algorithm. You can query CloudTrail with aws cloudtrail lookup-events to find all S3 writes in a time window, enabling audit trails of who uploaded what and with which checksum method.
explanation.why: CloudWatch Logs captures application/service logs but not API-level audit trails. Config tracks resource configuration state. Trusted Advisor provides best-practice recommendations.

questions.question: What is a pre-signed URL and how does it enforce checksum validation on untrusted uploads?

options.text: A permanent URL that allows anyone to download an S3 object without authentication
A temporary signed URL that grants time-limited upload/download access; when generated with x-amz-checksum-sha256, the upload is rejected if the client's data checksum does not match
A URL that automatically encrypts the uploaded file
A URL that compresses the file before uploading to S3

explanation.correct: A pre-signed URL embeds credentials and expiry into the URL itself — no AWS account needed to use it. When the server generates it with a checksum requirement (x-amz-checksum-sha256 header), any client uploading via that URL must provide the matching checksum or S3 rejects the upload. This is used in web applications where browsers upload directly to S3.
explanation.why: Pre-signed URLs are not permanent and do not encrypt or compress. They are the standard pattern for secure browser-to-S3 uploads in web applications.

questions.question: After configuring an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition objects to S3 Glacier after 30 days, what happens to the stored checksum?

options.text: The checksum is deleted when the object moves to Glacier
The checksum is recalculated after the transition
The checksum is preserved through all storage class transitions — S3 maintains integrity metadata across tiers
Glacier does not support checksums — you must re-upload to add one

explanation.correct: S3 checksum metadata persists through all storage class transitions — Standard to Standard-IA to Glacier Deep Archive. The ChecksumSHA256 field remains in object metadata at every tier. This means a long-term archive can still be integrity-verified years after original upload.
explanation.why: Storage class transitions change where S3 stores the data physically, not the metadata associated with the object. Integrity guarantees apply at all tiers.

questions.question: What does S3 Inventory provide for integrity monitoring at scale?

options.text: A real-time API that returns checksums for all objects on demand
A scheduled daily or weekly CSV/Parquet report listing every object with its checksum, size, storage class, and encryption status
An automated alert when checksums change
A comparison tool that downloads and re-verifies all objects

explanation.correct: S3 Inventory generates a scheduled flat-file report (CSV or Parquet) of every object in a bucket including ChecksumAlgorithm, ChecksumType, ETag, Size, LastModified, StorageClass, and EncryptionStatus. For buckets with millions of objects this is far more efficient than calling head-object per object — the report lands in a destination bucket and can be queried with Athena.
explanation.why: Inventory is pull-based and scheduled, not real-time. For real-time validation use Lambda + S3 Event Notifications. For batch audit at scale use Inventory + Athena.

questions.question: A Lambda function triggered by S3 Event Notifications receives an ObjectCreated event. Which API call retrieves the stored checksum for the new object without incurring egress charges?

options.text: s3.getObject()
s3.headObject()
s3.getObjectAttributes()
Both B and C are valid zero-egress options

explanation.correct: Both headObject and getObjectAttributes return metadata without transferring object data — zero egress cost. headObject returns the full metadata block including ChecksumSHA256. getObjectAttributes returns only specific attributes you request (Checksum, ETag, ObjectSize) — slightly more efficient for large-scale Lambda invocations.
explanation.why: getObject downloads the full object data — always incurs egress and is too expensive for integrity monitoring at scale. headObject and getObjectAttributes are both correct zero-egress options.

questions.question: In a performance benchmark comparing SHA-256 vs CRC32-C for 100 uploads of a 10 MB file, CRC32-C is expected to be faster. Why?

options.text: CRC32-C uses a 32-bit output vs SHA-256's 256-bit output, making the hash shorter to transmit
CRC32-C uses a polynomial specifically optimized for hardware instruction sets (SSE4.2 on Intel/AMD, CRC32 instructions on ARM), completing calculation in hardware rather than software
CRC32-C skips some bytes in the file to calculate faster
AWS gives CRC32-C uploads higher network priority than SHA-256 uploads

explanation.correct: CRC32-C (Castagnoli) uses the CRC32 hardware instruction available on all modern x86 (SSE4.2) and ARM processors. The hash is calculated in dedicated silicon rather than general CPU instructions — this is 10-40x faster than SHA-256's purely software computation for equivalent file sizes.
explanation.why: The output size difference (32-bit vs 256-bit) is negligible for transmission. CRC32-C speed advantage comes entirely from hardware acceleration — not from a smaller output or any shortcut in file coverage.

questions.question: What is the minimum CloudTrail configuration required to capture S3 data events like PutObject?

options.text: CloudTrail is automatically enabled for all S3 events — no configuration needed
Create a trail with Data Events enabled for S3, selecting 'All S3 buckets' or specific bucket ARNs
Enable S3 Server Access Logging — this captures the same events as CloudTrail
Enable AWS Config rules for S3 — Config automatically feeds CloudTrail

explanation.correct: CloudTrail by default only captures management events (bucket creation, policy changes). To capture data events like PutObject, GetObject, and DeleteObject, you must explicitly enable Data Events in your trail configuration for S3. Without this, object-level API calls are not logged.
explanation.why: S3 Server Access Logging captures HTTP access logs but lacks the structured JSON format and IAM context that CloudTrail provides. Config tracks configuration state, not individual API calls.

questions.question: You generate a pre-signed URL for a partner company to upload a file to your S3 bucket. The upload succeeds but head-object shows no ChecksumSHA256. What must you add to the pre-signed URL generation?

options.text: The partner must have an AWS account to add checksums
Include ChecksumAlgorithm='SHA256' in the presign parameters — this forces the client to send and S3 to validate the checksum header
Pre-signed URLs cannot enforce checksums — use a different upload method
Set the Content-Type header to sha256 during upload

explanation.correct: When generating the pre-signed URL, include ChecksumAlgorithm in the presign parameters. This creates a URL that requires the client to include the x-amz-checksum-sha256 header with their calculated checksum. S3 validates this on receipt. Without it, the upload succeeds but no checksum is stored.
explanation.why: Pre-signed URLs can absolutely enforce checksums — this is the correct pattern for partner/browser uploads where you need integrity guarantees without exposing AWS credentials.

questions.question: An S3 Inventory report includes ChecksumAlgorithm and ChecksumType columns. What does ChecksumType='FULL_OBJECT' mean versus 'COMPOSITE'?

options.text: FULL_OBJECT means the checksum covers the entire file in one calculation; COMPOSITE means it was calculated over multipart upload parts and combined
FULL_OBJECT means SHA-256 was used; COMPOSITE means CRC32-C was used
FULL_OBJECT is for files under 5GB; COMPOSITE is for files over 5GB
Both types are identical — the distinction is cosmetic

explanation.correct: FULL_OBJECT means the checksum was calculated over the complete file content in a single operation — used for single-part uploads. COMPOSITE means the checksum is derived from the checksums of individual multipart upload parts — the composite is SHA-256 of the concatenated part checksums, not SHA-256 of the file itself.
explanation.why: This distinction matters for validation scripts: a COMPOSITE checksum cannot be verified by running sha256sum on the assembled file locally. You must validate at the part level or use AWS tools that understand composite checksums.

questions.question: Which combination of tools provides the most complete real-time integrity monitoring system for an S3 bucket receiving hundreds of uploads per hour?

options.text: Manual nightly batch script using the CLI
S3 Inventory daily report queried with Athena
S3 Event Notifications → Lambda (validates checksum, stores result in DynamoDB) → SNS alert on FAIL
CloudTrail + Config rules

explanation.correct: S3 Event Notifications trigger Lambda within seconds of each upload. Lambda calls headObject to retrieve the stored checksum, compares against the expected baseline in DynamoDB, writes the PASS/FAIL result back to DynamoDB, and publishes to SNS if a FAIL is detected. This architecture is event-driven, scales automatically, and catches failures within 60 seconds — not the next morning.
explanation.why: Nightly batch scripts have an overnight blind window. Inventory is scheduled daily, not real-time. CloudTrail + Config can detect configuration changes but not per-object data integrity failures.
